paragraphs: Decision center: the work of detectives and criminal investigators is to turn a report or lead into a verifiable, reproducible evidence chain that can withstand court scrutiny — interviewing witnesses and suspects, checking records to verify identity, securing and searching the scene, recording and preserving evidence, analyzing reports to determine the next steps, and preparing warrants and court materials. The focus of judgment is not whether you look like a detective, but whether every step on the chain of intake and verification — evidence collection and preservation — analysis and applications — giving evidence and appearing in court is documented and traceable.

Worth trying first: you can patiently check contradictions between testimony and records item by item, are willing to fill in and preserve evidence records according to procedure, can stay careful through long surveillance and repeated questioning, can accept a way of working that is supervised by law and constrained by time limits and approvals, and can write conclusions into reports that others can review.

Requires caution: if you are impatient with procedure and paperwork, tend to jump to conclusions by intuition, or find it hard to stay restrained in stressful and emotional situations (victims, families, suspects), or expect to take coercive measures at any time without being subject to approval and supervision, then the actual work experience usually does not match expectations.

Low-risk verification: use fictional case material to complete an exercise in arranging one report and three witness statements into a timeline and a list of contradictions, writing out the facts and evidence points that need verification, and writing a paragraph on investigation progress and next steps according to given elements; this only verifies whether you are willing to check and document item by item according to procedure. The exercise uses fictional material and involves no real case, no real investigation, evidence collection or coercive measures, and does not equal hiring, training or law enforcement qualification.

Decision center: whether report information, scene traces and statements from multiple parties can be arranged into a chain of evidence and reports that colleagues can understand, that can later be reproduced, and that can withstand legal scrutiny.

The work is mainly investigation and communication: dealing with external customers or the public accounts for 100% (extremely important), email 100% every day, telephone conversation 100% every day, face-to-face discussion with individuals and teams 84% every day, continuous contact with others 90%; the importance of precision or accuracy is 99% (extremely important), the consequence of error 82% (extremely serious), a typical workweek longer than 40 hours 67%, outdoor exposure to various weather conditions 60% every day; very high responsibility for the health and safety of other employees 68%, and decisions having a very important impact on the results of colleagues or the unit 84%. Scenes, interview rooms, offices and courtrooms alternate, and the pace is determined by case progress and statutory time limits.

Similar names do not mean the same duties: this page is O*NET-SOC 33-3021.00 Detectives and Criminal Investigators, whose core is conducting investigations into suspected unlawful conduct to prevent or solve crime; adjacent positions have different duties — patrol officers handle front-line patrol, taking reports and initial response (this occupation often takes over cases they refer), forensic science technicians handle laboratory examination and technical analysis, intelligence analysts handle intelligence assessment, police identification and records officers handle fingerprints and criminal records, and private detectives have no law enforcement powers or coercive measures. Specific authority is governed by the position, statutory powers and approval procedures, and is not inferred from the job title.

Inputs that must be verified: the content of the report or complaint, scene protection and the surrounding area, statements of witnesses and parties, the source of physical evidence and custody and transfer records, the records and files to be checked, the applicable approvals for opening a case and for coercive measures, and the statutory time limits and case procedures. What must not be done: do not take coercive measures such as search or arrest without approval, do not let others disturb the body or the scene before forensic staff arrive, do not omit sealing, marking and transfer records for evidence, do not write unverified statements as conclusions, and do not use investigation information for non-case purposes.

Fit judgments should be made in combination with the accuracy of procedural execution, the quality of paperwork and evidence records, patience during multiple rounds of questioning and long surveillance, and acceptance of a way of working that is supervised by law, and should not be replaced by a self-assessment of investigative flair or personal heroism; these all need to be confirmed in training and actual casework.

All paper exercises on this page use fictional material; real investigation, questioning, evidence collection, search, arrest, surveillance and court appearances must be carried out by personnel who have lawfully obtained law enforcement qualifications and are bound by statutory procedure and approval (for example, people's police in mainland China recruited through public examination and having completed training; in the United States, by the rules of each law enforcement agency and jurisdiction). Individuals must not conduct investigations or take coercive measures on their own, and this page does not constitute compliance or legal advice.

The object of this occupation's work is case facts and evidence: the content of reports and complaints, statements of witnesses and parties, scene traces and physical evidence, records and file data, and the resulting evidence chain and investigation reports; the outputs are investigation records and reports, warrants and court materials, and evidence custody and transfer records; the basis for judgment is statutory case procedure, evidence standards and approval authority, not personal inference or job title.

Judgment one: whether the case facts are verified item by item — whether there are contradictions between statements and records, and whether cross-verification is done by checking records and questioning multiple parties rather than accepting a single account.

Judgment two: whether the scene and evidence are correctly preserved — whether the scene is cordoned off and the surrounding area checked, whether the body and physical evidence are protected before others can touch them, and whether traces are recorded, marked, photographed and measured.

Judgment three: whether the evidence chain is complete and traceable — whether the source, sealing, marking, transfer and examination records of physical evidence are continuous, since a gap at any step may affect its probative value.

Articles 3 / 4 / 19 of the Criminal Procedure Law divide direct investigation duties by law among public security, procuratorial and state security bodies and other legal duties, and do not make all investigation the exclusive preserve of public security police; Article 12: no one may be found guilty without a court judgment. Article 50: evidence must be verified as true; Article 52: evidence of guilt, innocence and of aggravation or mitigation must be collected and unlawful methods are prohibited; Article 54: secrets and privacy must be kept confidential; Article 56: unlawful verbal evidence is excluded, and where the procedure for physical or documentary evidence is unlawful and may seriously affect justice it must be corrected with a reasonable explanation, otherwise it is excluded — this is not automatic exclusion for any missing record. Article 138: a search warrant is normally produced, but in emergencies when executing an arrest or detention it need not be used separately; the branches of specific statutory measures must be verified separately, and they cannot be approved arbitrarily by the individual or a superior.

Judgment five: whether the investigation report can be reviewed — whether conclusions are built on verified facts and state what information still needs to be added and what the next steps are, so that colleagues and supervisors can review on that basis.

Judgment six: whether collaboration and information exchange follow the rules — whether information exchange with laboratories, other agencies and prosecutors follows procedure, and whether case information and personal information are protected from misuse.

The work of detectives and criminal investigators can be divided into three linked but independent work areas. The first is case intake and lead verification: obtaining facts or statements from complainants, witnesses and accused persons and recording interviews, checking records and government agency files to find identity data on suspects, analyzing completed reports to determine what information and investigative work are still needed, and determining the scope, timing and direction of the investigation. The second is scene and evidence handling: cordoning off or roping off the scene and checking the surrounding area, organizing the scene search and assigning tasks and areas to officers, recording, marking and photographing objects found at the scene and measuring the scene, searching for and collecting evidence such as fingerprints, preserving, processing and analyzing evidence items, checking the victim's vital signs and calling for medical assistance, and preventing others from disturbing the body before forensic staff arrive. The third is analysis and case delivery: recording investigation progress and maintaining suspect information files, submitting reports to superiors or a magistrate to apply for warrants, preparing and serving search and arrest warrants, testifying before a grand jury about criminal activity investigations, preparing charges or defences and materials for court cases according to formal procedure, and collaborating with other agencies, keeping surveillance or carrying out undercover assignments. The three work areas proceed according to statutory procedure, and the pace is determined by case progress and statutory time limits.

Where are the boundaries between detectives and criminal investigators and patrol officers, forensic staff, intelligence analysts and private detectives?

The editor compares by main focus: this page investigates suspected unlawful conduct; patrol officers maintain order, take reports and respond, and also handle accident and crime investigations; forensic science technicians collect, identify and classify and analyze physical evidence at the scene or in the laboratory and may testify; intelligence analysts analyze leads to anticipate and prevent crime; police identification and records officers cover scene photography, fingerprint and trace examination, evidence packaging, custody and analysis and court testimony, and not merely criminal record keeping. Private detectives conduct investigations for clients, and the job title does not grant public coercive powers. The tasks overlap, and qualification, authority and statutory procedure must be verified separately by jurisdiction.
Core purpose
Establish the facts of a case, collect and preserve evidence, and provide credible grounds for lawful handling and judicial proceedings.

Main focus: patrol officers cover order and incident response as well as investigation; forensic science technicians collect and analyze physical evidence; intelligence analysts anticipate and prevent crime; identification and records officers collect, keep and analyze scene evidence and fingerprints; private detectives conduct commissioned investigations.
Main objects and basis

The objects are the content of reports and complaints, statements and records, scene traces and physical evidence, and the resulting evidence chain; the basis is statutory case procedure, evidence standards and approval authority.

Main objects: patrol incidents and accidents and suspicious activity; scene physical evidence, traces, fingerprints and images for forensic science and identification record positions; multi-source crime leads for intelligence analysts; lawful commissioned matters for private detectives. The specific methods and authority depend on the position and jurisdiction, and scene and laboratory are not absolutely mutually exclusive.
Core process
Intake and verification → scene and evidence collection → analysis and comparison → applying for warrants and investigative measures → case delivery and court appearance → archiving.

Editorial comparison: patrol, incident response and necessary investigation; forensic science positions collect, preserve and examine evidence at the scene; identification and records positions photograph the scene, lift traces and fingerprints, package and submit or analyze evidence and testify; intelligence analysts collect and analyze crime leads; private detectives conduct commissioned investigations. This is not a uniform process across units.
Main outputs
Interview and investigation records, scene records and photographs, evidence sealing and transfer inventories, warrants and court materials, investigation reports.

Main outputs may include patrol incident and investigation handling records; forensic science technical reports and evidence analysis; intelligence assessment products; scene photographs, physical evidence and fingerprint analysis, evidence records and court statements for identification and records positions; and commissioned investigation reports for private detectives. This is not a list of mutually exclusive outputs.
Responsible parties

People in this occupation are responsible for the lawfulness, truthfulness and completeness of the investigation process and evidence, and exercise their powers within the scope of authorization; measures and coercive measures beyond authorization require statutory approval and must not be decided unilaterally.

Each adjacent position is responsible within its own duties for order response, investigation, scene evidence collection, technical analysis, evidence custody, assessment or commissioned investigation; identification and records officers do more than maintain files. Overlapping focus and tasks do not mean that qualification, technical conclusions or coercive powers are mutually recognized.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate with patrol police, laboratories, other law enforcement and administrative agencies, prosecutors and the courts, exchange information according to procedure and accept supervision by supervisors and statutory approvals; when a matter exceeds one's authorization or the evidence is insufficient, ask first and supplement the investigation.

Collaboration of adjacent positions: patrol officers collaborate with command and the dispatch centre; forensic staff collaborate with case officers and examination bodies; intelligence analysts collaborate with all operational departments; records officers collaborate with front-line and case units; private detectives collaborate with the client.

What are the common misconceptions about the occupation of detective and criminal investigator?

Common misconceptions include: thinking the work is mainly deduction and arrests, while ignoring the large amount of procedural paperwork, evidence custody and approval steps; thinking search or interrogation can be done at will, while ignoring that coercive measures require lawful approval and must be used within the scope of authorization; confusing it with patrol officers, forensic staff or private detectives; thinking conclusions are reached by intuition, while ignoring cross-verification and court scrutiny requirements; and ignoring that the consequences of error are extremely serious (82%) and the requirement for precision (99%). The direction comparison first fixes one thing: the law enforcement and investigation process is divided by who handles front-line incident response and initial handling, who handles case investigation and evidence collection, who handles technical examination, and who handles intelligence assessment; the occupation on this page (O*NET-SOC 33-3021.00 Detectives and Criminal Investigators) sits in the case investigation and evidence collection segment. First consider which segment of responsibility you are more willing to take on, then compare with adjacent positions.

Process direction one, case intake and lead verification: obtaining facts or statements from complainants, witnesses and accused persons and recording interviews, checking records and government agency files to find identity data on suspects, analyzing completed reports to determine what information and investigative work are still needed, and determining the scope, timing and direction of the investigation; this is the segment that opens first after this occupation takes on a case and the one most sensitive to cross-verification and recording ability.

Process direction two, scene and evidence handling: cordoning off or roping off the scene and checking the surrounding area, organizing the scene search and assigning tasks and areas, recording, marking and photographing scene objects and measuring the scene, searching for and collecting evidence such as fingerprints, preserving, processing and analyzing evidence items, and sealing, keeping and submitting them for examination according to procedure. This segment places more emphasis on scene discipline, continuity of the evidence chain and complete formalities.

Adjacent positions: Police and Sheriff's Patrol Officers (O*NET-SOC 33-3051.00) and First-Line Supervisors of Police and Detectives. The former handle front-line patrol, taking reports and initial response, and this occupation often takes over the cases and leads they refer; the latter handle command, supervision and resource allocation in investigation and police work. Compared with them, the occupation on this page focuses more on individual case investigation, evidence collection and case delivery.
Process direction: case intake and lead verification (one of the core work areas of the occupation on this page)

Obtain the content of the report and complaint, question witnesses and accused persons and record interviews, check records and government agency files to find identity data on suspects, analyze completed reports to identify the information and investigative work needed, and determine the scope, timing and direction of the investigation.

Compared with patrol positions, this segment centres on proactive investigation and cross-verification and is not limited to scene response; compared with intelligence analysis, this segment centres on individual case facts and evidence, and its conclusions must be able to enter judicial proceedings and be reviewed.

If you are willing to deal with statements, records and contradictions over the long term and can accept a large amount of procedural paperwork, you can make case intake and lead verification your main line.
Process direction: scene and evidence handling

Cordon off or rope off the scene and check the surrounding area, organize the scene search and assign tasks and areas, record, mark and photograph scene objects and measure the scene, search for and collect evidence such as fingerprints, and seal, keep and submit evidence items for examination.

Compared with laboratory technical positions, this segment completes collection and preservation at the scene, and examination and analysis are carried out by forensic and other technical staff; compared with patrol positions, this segment emphasises continuity of the evidence chain and complete formalities rather than the immediate maintenance of scene order.
If you are more interested in the scene, traces and preservation of physical evidence, you can make scene and evidence handling your main line.
Adjacent positions: patrol officers (33-3051.00) and first-line supervisors

Patrol officers handle front-line patrol, taking reports and initial response and are responsible for scene order; first-line supervisors handle command, supervision and resource allocation and are usually promoted from experienced police personnel. The scope of responsibility and the powers they exercise differ from the occupation on this page and must be distinguished by position and statutory authority.

If you want to build up scene response and police experience first, you can start from a patrol position and then move into investigation; if you want to take on organizational and supervisory responsibility, you should aim at first-line supervisor.
Adjacent positions: forensic science technicians (19-4092.00) and intelligence analysts (33-3021.06)

Forensic science technicians receive samples, conduct examinations and technical analysis and issue examination conclusions; intelligence analysts collect and assess intelligence to support decisions and investigations. The occupation on this page sits in the investigation and evidence collection stage, and examination conclusions and intelligence products are important inputs rather than its outputs.

If you prefer dealing with instruments, samples and examination methods, you can compare the forensic science direction; if you prefer dealing with data and intelligence assessment, you can compare the intelligence analysis direction.
Adjacent positions: private detectives and investigators (33-9021.00) and correctional officers

Private detectives conduct private investigations for commissioned matters and have no law enforcement powers or coercive measures; correctional officers supervise and reform detainees, and their work setting is a custodial institution. Both differ clearly from the occupation on this page in the source of authority, coercive means and work setting.
If you prefer private commissioned investigation, you can compare the private detective direction; if you prefer work in custodial institutions, you can compare the corrections direction.
Boundary explanation: preparation level, law enforcement authorization and examination recruitment

The preparation level for this occupation in the United States is Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), usually requiring 1—2 years of training; the BLS Occupational Outlook (Police and Detectives broad group) lists medium-term on-the-job training, with most having first graduated from their agency's training academy and usually being required to be at least 21 years old and to pass strict physical fitness and personal condition screening. Investigative work in mainland China is carried out by people's police who have lawfully obtained law enforcement qualifications, who must meet the conditions set out in the People's Police Law of the People's Republic of China and are generally recruited through public examination (including physical fitness assessment, medical examination and political vetting). Investigative measures and coercive measures must all be exercised within the scope of statutory authorization and approval, and authority must not be exceeded.

When choosing, look at the source of the position's law enforcement authorization, the range of investigative and coercive measures that may be exercised, the training and screening requirements, and whether it is subject to statutory approval and supervision, rather than only the job title and pay figures.

entries.answer: Detectives and criminal investigators investigate conduct suspected of violating federal, state or local law in order to prevent or solve crime: obtaining facts or statements from complainants, witnesses and accused persons and recording interviews, checking records and government agency files to verify identity and connections, and determining the scope, timing and direction of the investigation; cordoning off or roping off the scene and checking the surrounding area, organizing the scene search, recording, marking and photographing scene objects and measuring the scene, searching for and collecting evidence, and preserving, processing and analyzing evidence items; recording investigation progress and maintaining suspect files, submitting reports to apply for warrants, preparing and serving search and arrest warrants within the scope of authorization, testifying before a grand jury about criminal activity investigations, and preparing charges or defences and court case materials according to procedure.
entries.question: What do detectives and criminal investigators actually do every day?

entries.answer: The three divide the work differently: the occupation on this page is responsible for individual case investigation, evidence collection and case delivery; patrol officers handle front-line patrol, taking reports and initial response and are responsible for scene order, and this occupation often takes over the cases they refer; forensic science technicians receive samples and conduct examination and analysis and issue examination conclusions. The specific duties, statutory authority and approval procedures are governed by the job description, agency standards and applicable regulations and cannot be exchanged by job title.

entries.answer: This page does not give a substitution conclusion. Tools such as case and record retrieval, image processing and document assistance are already used in some steps, but the impact of generative AI on specific tasks requires task-level evidence, and this page does not give a substitution ratio or date.
entries.question: How will AI and automation affect detectives and criminal investigators?

entries.answer: The verifiable technical directions are retrieval and comparison of case and record data, queries of identity and criminal record databases, digitisation and organization of scene and surveillance images, image recording of traces and physical evidence, and text organization and assisted drafting of interviews and reports; these are tool and system capabilities and do not equal general adoption or position outcomes. entries.answer: Priority verification: whether facts are cross-verified item by item, whether the scene and physical evidence are preserved as required, whether the evidence chain is continuous and traceable, whether query and comparison results have been reviewed by a person, whether investigative measures and coercive measures are approved according to law, and whether investigation records and documents are complete and truthful; these steps must currently still be verified and signed by personnel with law enforcement qualification and authorization.

entries.answer: The preparation level for this occupation is Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), usually requiring 1—2 years of training; O*NET feedback on the education requirements of newly hired personnel is a postsecondary certificate 26%, high school or equivalent 23%, and some college with no degree 20%. The BLS Occupational Outlook (Police and Detectives broad group) lists medium-term on-the-job training, with most having first graduated from their agency's training academy and usually being required to be at least 21 years old and to pass strict physical fitness and personal condition screening. Actual competence depends more on procedural compliance capability and the quality of evidence preservation and documents.
entries.question: What education and training are needed?

entries.answer: There is no uniform national licence in the United States, and requirements vary with the agency and jurisdiction (most must first graduate from an agency training academy and complete on-the-job training). Investigative work in mainland China is carried out by people's police who have lawfully obtained law enforcement qualifications: they must meet the conditions in Article twenty-six of the People's Police Law of the People's Republic of China (at least eighteen years old, upholding the Constitution, good political, professional and personal conduct, good health, a high school education or above, and willingness to work as people's police; those who have previously been criminally punished or dismissed from public office may not serve), and are generally recruited through public examination, including physical fitness assessment, medical examination and political vetting.

description.text: Detectives and Criminal Investigators (O*NET-SOC 33-3021.00) investigate conduct suspected of being unlawful in order to prevent or solve crime: obtaining the report and interviewing witnesses and accused persons, checking records and files to verify identity, determining the scope and direction of the investigation, cordoning off and checking the scene and organizing the search, recording, marking and photographing scene objects and measuring, searching for and collecting evidence, sealing, keeping and submitting physical evidence for examination, recording progress and submitting reports to apply for warrants, preparing and serving search and arrest warrants, and testifying in court and preparing court materials. The work is mainly investigation and communication: dealing with the public 100% extremely important, email and telephone conversation both 100% every day, continuous contact with others 90%, importance of precision or accuracy 99% extremely important, consequences of error 82% extremely serious, typical workweek over 40 hours 67%, outdoor exposure to various weather 60% every day. United States scope: in the 2025 wage data the median annual wage is 93,790 USD (median hourly 45.09 USD), with annual percentiles of 55,390 / 69,330 / 93,790 / 120,520 / 160,540 USD; 2024 employment is about 117,900 people, a decline is projected for 2024—2034 with about 7,800 projected openings; the interest code is ICR. Mainland China: investigative work is carried out by people's police who have lawfully obtained law enforcement qualifications, who must meet the conditions set out in the People's Police Law and are generally recruited through public examination with physical fitness assessment, medical examination and political vetting; public statistics have not established an occupational-level wage scope for this occupation, and this page marks the gap in the relevant places.

subject.name: Detectives and Criminal Investigators
subject.summary: Detectives and Criminal Investigators (O*NET-SOC 33-3021.00) are personnel who investigate conduct suspected of violating federal, state or local law in order to prevent or solve crime: obtaining facts or statements from complainants, witnesses and accused persons and recording interviews, checking records and government agency files to verify identity and connections, and determining the scope, timing and direction of the investigation; cordoning off or roping off the scene and checking the surrounding area, organizing the scene search and assigning tasks and areas, recording, marking and photographing scene objects and measuring the scene, searching for and collecting evidence such as fingerprints, and preserving, processing and analyzing evidence items; recording investigation progress and maintaining suspect files, submitting reports to superiors or a magistrate to apply for warrants, preparing and serving search and arrest warrants within the scope of authorization, testifying before a grand jury about criminal activity investigations, and preparing charges or defences and court case materials according to formal procedure, collaborating with other agencies and keeping surveillance or carrying out undercover assignments. United States scope: in the 2025 wage data for this occupation the median annual wage is 93,790 USD (median hourly 45.09 USD), with annual percentiles of 55,390 / 69,330 / 93,790 / 120,520 / 160,540 USD (hourly percentiles 26.63 / 33.33 / 45.09 / 57.94 / 77.18); 2024 employment is about 117,900 people, a decline is projected for 2024—2034 (-1% or lower) with about 7,800 projected openings; the BLS Occupational Outlook separately gives the Police and Detectives broad group as 824,200 positions in 2025, +3% for 2025—2035 and about 60,100 annual average openings; the preparation level is Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), usually requiring 1—2 years of training; the interest code is ICR; the work context includes dealing with the public 100% extremely important, email and telephone conversation both 100% every day, continuous contact with others 90%, importance of precision or accuracy 99% extremely important, consequences of error 82% extremely serious, typical workweek over 40 hours 67%, and outdoor exposure to various weather 60% every day. Mainland China scope: investigative work is carried out by people's police who have lawfully obtained law enforcement qualifications, who must meet the conditions set out in the People's Police Law of the People's Republic of China (at least eighteen years old, upholding the Constitution, good political, professional and personal conduct, good health, a high school education or above, and willingness to work as people's police; those who have previously been criminally punished or dismissed from public office may not serve), are generally recruited through public examination (including written examination, interview, physical fitness assessment, medical examination and political vetting), and are subject to a police rank system. Public statistics have not published occupational-level wages corresponding to this occupation, and this page retains the gap as it stands.
